headline: Trump asked China's Xi Jinping if he'd 'like to buy' American weapons, US ambassador reveals
trending_claim: Ambassador David Perdue said on Fox News Sunday that Trump asked Xi Jinping 'at one point' whether he would like to buy American weapons.
rating_explained: The Post's central claim is an attribution claim: that Ambassador David Perdue said on Fox News Sunday that President Trump asked Xi Jinping 'at one point' whether he would like to buy American weapons. The Associated Press (Ben Finley, syndicated Sept. 27-28) reported the identical quote verbatim: Perdue, speaking to Shannon Bream on 'Fox News Sunday' days after Trump hosted Xi for a state visit, said, 'He actually asked President Xi, would he like to buy some, at one point.' AP notes Perdue did not specify when the offer was made and was responding to questions about delayed Taiwan arms packages. The Wall Street Journal independently quoted the same line in its Sept. 28 follow-up. The White House has not clarified whether Trump was serious. The verdict is accurate because the Post's claim is precisely that Perdue said it, and that is confirmed word-for-word by two independent wire/newsroom sources. One caveat: whether Trump actually made the offer to Xi is unconfirmed by any source — Perdue said it, and the Post reports only that he said it, so the attribution holds.
trending_context: On Sept. 28, Politomix showed the story with 118 shares; the same claim was picked up the same day by AP syndication, the Wall Street Journal, Reuters, and the New York Times.

headline: U.S. Says No Plans to Sell Weapons to China After Perdue Comments
trending_claim: U.S. officials said the Trump administration has no plans to sell weapons to China, and that such sales are already prohibited by law.
rating_explained: The Journal's central claim is that Trump administration officials said the U.S. has no plans to sell weapons to Beijing after Ambassador Perdue's Sunday remarks, and that such sales are already prohibited by law. This is confirmed by New York Times reporting (Edward Wong): the White House said through a U.S. official that the United States had no plans to sell arms to China, and the State Department said in a statement, 'U.S. law prohibits arms sales to China and there is no offer or plan to sell arms to China.' The legal prohibition is the longstanding post-1989 arms embargo on China, codified in U.S. law (Section 902 of the Foreign Relations Authorization Act for FY1990-1991, per CRS documentation cited by analysts covering the story). The Journal's two on-the-record U.S. officials match the NYT's account of the White House and State Department positions. The verdict is accurate: both halves of the claim — no plans, and a legal prohibition — are confirmed by named official statements carried by independent newsrooms.

sources.name: New York Times (via TAM synthesis of NYT World)

trending_context: Updated about an hour before the Sept. 28 search; it is the administration's on-the-record response to Perdue's Sunday remarks, which were the day's most-shared China story.

headline: Zelensky says Trump has made 'final decision' to allow Kyiv to make Patriot missiles
trending_claim: Zelensky said Trump made a 'final decision' to grant Ukraine a license to manufacture Patriot missiles.
rating_explained: CNN's central claim is an attribution claim: that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told reporters on Friday, September 25, that Trump had emphasized to him, 'yes, I have made the final decision: Ukraine will receive a license to manufacture Patriot missiles.' The Washington Examiner confirmed Zelensky made these statements Friday at the UN General Assembly, quoting him: 'There are concrete agreements in place,' and the same 'final decision' line. Signal Post News independently reported the same Zelensky account. The story also properly notes the unresolved underlying question: the Washington Examiner reported Trump 'has not referenced such a promise' and that it had reached out to the White House and State Department for comment; Signal Post News reported Trump declined to confirm the license when CNN asked him directly on Saturday, September 26, saying only that he and Zelensky discussed Patriots. The verdict is accurate because CNN's claim is that Zelensky said it — and he did, per multiple outlets. The underlying question of whether Trump actually made the final decision remains unconfirmed by the White House, and CNN itself flagged that it had approached the White House for comment, so the piece does not overstate the evidence.
trending_context: Carried by CNN, the New York Post, and AFP syndication on Sept. 25-27, with follow-up coverage on Sept. 26 noting the White House did not confirm the license.

headline: Iran condemns Trump's 'hateful and disgusting' threats in UN complaint
trending_claim: Iran's UN envoy quoted Trump as saying 'I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly' in a letter to the UN secretary-general and Security Council president.
rating_explained: CORRECTION (Sept. 28): this story was re-verified under a stricter standard — a claim is only rated 'accurate' when the underlying event is confirmed by direct evidence, not merely because an outlet reported that it happened. The quotes attributed to Trump in the complaint are real and verified verbatim against his September 22 UNGA remarks (Christian Post, CNN, AP). However, the letter's dispatch to the secretary-general and Security Council president is single-sourced to Press TV (Iranian state media); a recheck found no UN document, IRNA item, or independent corroboration that the letter was sent. The event itself therefore remains unverified, so the verdict moves from 'accurate' to 'mostly-accurate'. Press TV's central claim is that Iran's UN envoy, Gholamhossein Darzi, sent a letter to UN Secretary-General Guterres and the Security Council president condemning Trump's September 22 UNGA remarks and quoting him. The quotes in the complaint are verified against Trump's actual speech. Trump's words, as reported by the Christian Post (Sept. 22), CNN (Sept. 26), and the Associated Press (Sept. 23): 'I have a big decision to make... Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again? Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?' Press TV's rendering — 'I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly' and 'drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness' — is a slight compression (dropping 'do' and 'or generations'), but the substance is identical. One context note: Trump framed the remarks as a question within a 'big decision' (deal vs. annihilation), which Press TV presents more flatly. The letter's existence is reported by Press TV; it is consistent with Darzi's established pattern of such letters (IRNA documented a September 2 Darzi letter to the UNSG) and with Foreign Minister Araghchi's public response to the same speech. The verdict is accurate: the quotes attributed to Trump in the complaint are real and verified verbatim by named sources.

sources.name: Christian Post (Trump UNGA speech transcript quotes)

trending_context: Published Sept. 28; search results on Sept. 28 showed it updated about eight hours earlier, citing Trump's Sept. 22 UN General Assembly address.

headline: Iran War Wounded Count Jumps to 861 as Pentagon Stays Silent, Trump Touts Unverified Ukraine Death Tolls

rating_explained: Unbiased Headlines' central claim is that President Trump told reporters on Saturday, September 26, that 25,000 people died in the Ukraine-Russia war last month, 32,000 the month before ('mostly soldiers, 97% soldiers'), and 33,000 two months ago — and that he cited no source. Fox News Digital's original reporting quotes him verbatim: 'Last month, 25,000 people died in the Ukraine-Russia war, okay? 25,000... The month before that, 32,000 people died... mostly soldiers, 97% soldiers... Two months ago, 33,000 people; this month, 25,000 people died. What a shame.' Multiple mirrors of the Fox piece (NY Times Post, RealTalk Digest, Cybernistas) carry the same quotes. Trump provided no methodology, battlefield audit, or third-party source. For scale: the Center for Strategic and International Studies estimates Russia alone has lost up to 450,000 soldiers cumulatively since the 2022 invasion — Trump's single-month figures would equal roughly a fifth of that entire 3.5-year cumulative estimate in one month, and no independent tracker cited in available reporting supports monthly death tolls of that magnitude. The verdict is accurate: the story's claim is that Trump made these unsourced claims, and both halves — that he said it, and that he gave no source — are verified by named sources.

headline: Trump DOJ Claims It Complied With Latest Epstein Order in Katie Phang Case
trending_claim: The Justice Department says Attorney General Todd Blanche complied with Judge Emmet Sullivan's September 16 order by turning over, for in-camera review, redacted and unredacted handwritten FBI notes from four interviews with a woman alleging Donald Trump sexually and physically abused her when she was 13 to 15; the judge has not yet confirmed what redaction-support material was submitted.

The verdict is accurate: the story's claim (DOJ says it complied; judge hasn't confirmed the redaction-support material) matches the verified record, including its own stated uncertainty.

headline: 'Sloppy and lazy': Kash Patel humiliated after teen hackers breach the FBI and steal personal info of thousands of agents
trending_claim: Teen hackers (ShinyHunters) breached FBI internal systems and stole personal data of thousands of FBI agents -- stated as fact in the piece, while Reuters/AP reporting only partially verified sample records and had not established that the data came from FBI internal systems.
rating_explained: The UnPresidented piece states as established fact — in its headline and body — that ShinyHunters 'breached the FBI' and 'stole a massive collection of sensitive data from the agency, including the personal information of thousands of agents.' The named-source record does not support that framing. Reuters (Raphael Satter and AJ Vicens, Sept. 22) reported the group's claim and partially verified a sample of ~5,000 records — finding matches in at least 10 instances, including FBI Director Kash Patel, by running details against credit bureau records and the dark-web intelligence firm District 4 Labs — but explicitly wrote: 'the news agency could not establish where the data came from, or whether it had been stolen from the FBI's internal systems as the hackers claimed.' 404 Media, which first reported the claim, similarly verified only that some sample records matched real people via OSINT tools. The FBI's September 23 statement said it is 'aware of claims regarding unauthorized activity affecting FBIjobs.gov and is currently investigating' and, per cybersecurity outlet SecurityAffairs, the agency has not determined whether the point of breach was a third party or its own enterprise and has not confirmed its internal systems were compromised. The verdict is misleading rather than false: the piece's core assertion (the FBI was breached and thousands of agents' data stolen) is presented as fact, while every named source — including the Reuters reporting the piece itself cites — stops at 'claimed' and explicitly says the source of the data is unconfirmed.
trending_context: Published Sept 27 (search showed updated 1 day before Sept 28); the alleged breach appeared in weekend progressive commentary (e.g., a MeidasTouch Sept 26 video segment) and partial verification reporting by Reuters/AP kept it in the news cycle. Note: trending evidence is thinner than the other items; included as the 'suspicious claim' slot.

headline: Two senior FBI agents ousted over investigation into alleged harassing calls to wife of Trump adviser Stephen Miller
trending_claim: FBI counterterrorism supervisors Michael Burgwald and Courtland Rae were removed and reassigned after their team found Katie Miller's alleged harassing calls did not meet the threshold for an FBI investigation and had no terrorism nexus; FBI official Darren Cox confirmed the moves but denied Patel ordered them, while White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said leadership found they were 'stifling investigations into very serious threats.'
rating_explained: CNN's central claim is confirmed across its parts. Bloomberg Law first reported (Sept. 26) that Michael Burgwald, special agent in charge of counterterrorism at the FBI's Washington Field Office, and his deputy Courtland Rae were removed and reassigned over the handling of the Katie Miller harassing-calls investigation. CNN's two sources added the key detail that the field office team found the calls did not meet the threshold for an FBI investigation and identified no terrorism nexus — a point Bloomberg Law's original reporting did not include. FBI Washington Field Office chief Darren Cox confirmed the ousting in an on-record statement on the FBI's 'Rapid Response' account while denying Director Kash Patel ordered it: 'Director Patel did not order this decision... This was a personnel decision made at the Washington field office level alone.' White House spokesperson Lauren Bis's statement — that the Millers never interacted with the two officials and that 'senior leadership at the FBI determined they were stifling investigations into very serious threats' — was confirmed by Bloomberg Law's reporting as relayed by multiple outlets (WLT Report, AllChronology). The exact reason for the removals is contested between CNN's anonymous sources and the White House's on-record statement, and CNN presents both accounts without adjudicating between them. The verdict is accurate: every attributed element of the claim is verified by named sources.

sources.name: WLT Report (quoting Bloomberg Law's original reporting)

headline: Ex-CIA Official Warns Trump Risking 'Catastrophic Terrorist Event' in the U.S.
trending_claim: Retired senior CIA operations officer Marc Polymeropoulos warned on X that the Trump administration's shift of federal law enforcement from counterterrorism to immigration risks a 'mass casualty event,' citing ProPublica's analysis that DOJ dropped 23,000 criminal cases (including hundreds of terrorism investigations) in the first six months of Trump's term while opening 32,000 immigration cases.
rating_explained: The Chronicle's piece (an aggregation of Raw Story's reporting by David McAfee) makes two checkable claims. First, the ProPublica figures: confirmed directly. ProPublica's April 2026 analysis found the DOJ dropped more than 23,000 criminal cases in the first six months of Trump's second term — including more than 1,000 terrorism cases — while prosecuting 32,000 new immigration cases, nearly triple the Biden-administration pace (also summarized by Reason). The Chronicle's 'hundreds of terrorism investigations' is a conservative restatement of ProPublica's 'more than 1,000.' Second, the Polymeropoulos warning: the specific X post was not independently viewable, but the quoted language matches Polymeropoulos's on-the-record public position — NPR (Sept. 9, 2026) quoted him: 'I am afraid that counter-terrorism will not be a priority until a mass casualty event, and then it very much will be once again,' in the context of CT resources being shifted to the border. The Chronicle also notes he 'has been an outspoken Trump critic since leaving the agency,' giving relevant context. The headline's 'catastrophic terrorist event' paraphrases his actual 'mass casualty event' wording, but the body uses his words. The verdict is accurate: the ProPublica figures are fully verified and the attributed warning matches his confirmed public statements.
trending_context: Published Sept 27; ProPublica's declination figures were actively cited across critical outlets during the Sept 26-28 window (Raw Story, MeidasTouch), and the piece feeds the same weekend conversation as the trending FBI counterterrorism demotions story tracked on Memeorandum and Archynetys.

headline: Trump admin cancels funding for refugees, immigrants and others in move lawmakers argue is illegal
trending_claim: Trump sent a pocket-rescission package to Congress on Friday, September 25, canceling $810 million in already-appropriated spending — including $567 million for HHS Refugee and Entrant Assistance — in what critics call an unlawful end-run around Congress's power of the purse.
rating_explained: CNN's central claim is fully confirmed by named sources. Reuters (Sept. 25, Thomson Reuters): 'US President Donald Trump sought on Friday to unilaterally withhold more than $800 million in spending on immigration, race and education that Congress has approved,' via a rarely used 'pocket rescission' technique. Bloomberg Government confirmed the $810 million total and the $567 million cut to HHS's Office of Refugee Resettlement programs, with the remaining cuts spanning Commerce, Education, DHS, HUD, Justice, and international assistance. The Washington Examiner confirmed the same figures and the Friday-night timing. On the legality dispute, CNN attributes the 'illegal' characterization to lawmakers — verified: Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins (R-Maine) said on September 25 that Congress received the $810 million package 'without warning or consultation' and that 'any effort to rescind appropriated funds without congressional approval is a clear violation of the law'; the GAO has concluded pocket rescissions that withhold funds through expiration are unlawful. CNN also presents the White House's rationale ('most harmful government spending' under the Impoundment Control Act) and notes the prior-year $4.9 billion foreign-aid pocket rescission precedent. The verdict is accurate: the amounts, the timing, the mechanism, and the attributed criticism are all verified, and the piece presents both sides of the dispute.
trending_context: Major multi-outlet story on Sept 26-27 — covered same weekend by CBS, AP, Bloomberg Government, TIME/Yahoo, NY Post, and Daily Caller; bipartisan rebuke from Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins calling it 'a clear violation of the law.'

Named sources confirm every element: Reuters reported Sept 26 that the White House fact sheet established a 'US-China Super Intelligence (SI) Dialogue to exchange views on risks and benefits,' with the next exchange by November 2026, and a 'bilateral communication channel' for SI incidents, noting Trump entered the summit wanting to 'leave it exactly where it is.' Trump's Sept 26 remarks to reporters outside the White House — 'we had a big talk on SI, and he likes the idea of changing the name to SI, too' — match the quote the article attributes to him. No established fact-checker has rated this claim. One caveat: the article attributes the incident-channel agreement to both 'the Chinese Foreign Ministry and the White House,' while secondary reporting notes only the US side had publicly described it — a minor attribution point that does not undermine the story's core 'no breakthrough' conclusion.

Multiple outlets confirm the remark: PrimeTimer quotes the same Sept 27 quote ('We have the best, I guess you could say poverty... We have the best poverty numbers ever in the history of our country'), and the full statement quoted by WebIndia123 adds 'there's less poverty now than at any time in the history of our country.' So the piece's central claim — Trump made the claim and the official Census numbers back it — is factually correct; its mockery targets the awkward phrasing ('best poverty'), not a falsehood. No established fact-checker has rated this claim.

headline: 'TRUMP-ENDORSED' VANISHES: Florida GOP Nominee Quietly Strips President From Homepage as Race Tightens
trending_claim: Byron Donalds' campaign removed at least eight prominent Trump references (banner, donation button, photo, 'Enact the Trump Agenda') from his homepage in a redesign, while Trump called the reporting 'Another Fake Story' and announced two Florida rallies with Donalds.
rating_explained: The story asserts Donalds' site was redesigned with at least eight prominent Trump references removed. Newsmax (Sept 26) confirms the underlying website changes occurred: 'At least eight references to Trump were removed from the homepage during a recent redesign,' including the earlier 'Trump-endorsed Proven Conservative Fighter' headline, the photo of Donalds and his wife with Trump, and 'Enact the Trump Agenda' among campaign priorities; Trump's endorsement remains on a separate endorsements page. Reporting via the Miami Herald (cited by Newsmax) and Visualping's archived-site analysis confirms the removals, while the Tampa Bay Times confirms the redesign dropped the Trump photo and 'Enact the Trump Agenda,' and quotes Donalds calling it 'a stupid story.' Trump did call the reports a 'Fake Story': Newsmax quotes his Truth Social post — 'Another Fake Story is that a very close friend of mine, a man I endorsed very early, Byron Donalds, is taking me off his website and Campaign materials' — and confirms he said two Florida rallies for Donalds were scheduled and predicted they would be 'SOLD OUT!' The St. Pete Polls tie (Donalds 43.5%, Jolly 43.4%, Sept 15-17, 913 likely voters) is confirmed by the same sources. The article also hedges fairly: 'That does not necessarily mean Donalds has broken with Trump. There is no evidence that he has withdrawn his support.' No established fact-checker has rated this claim.

sources.name: Newsmax (Sept 26, Trump 'Fake Story' post and website changes)

trending_context: Trump's 449-word Truth Social denial on Sept. 26 drove the story; the Miami Herald and website-tracking firm Visualping documented the removed references via archived versions, and the race is tight (St. Pete Polls: Donalds 43.5%, Jolly 43.4%).

headline: Donald Trump Was Booed at the Texas-Tennessee Football Game
trending_claim: Trump was loudly booed by the Neyland Stadium crowd when introduced on the jumbotron during the Sept. 26 Texas-Tennessee game, though some cheers were also audible.
rating_explained: The story asserts 'boos rang through Neyland Stadium' after Trump's jumbotron introduction, 'though some cheers were also audible.' The booing is corroborated: People magazine reported Trump 'was loudly booed by some fans at Neyland Stadium when he appeared on the Jumbotron, as captured in video footage shared on social media,' and the Daily Beast reported 'a roar of boos audible over scattered applause.' However, the characterization of boos as dominant is contested by reporters who were in the stadium: the Houston Chronicle, the Austin American-Statesman and OutKick described applause and cheers; WVLT reporter Will Puckett described 'smattering of cheers and boos alike'; Breitbart reported 'a roar of approval'; and PBS relayed 'cheers' from a text pool report. USA Today's For The Win assessed the booing claim: 'It doesn't appear so, at least not loudly.' An independent audit of 23 source documents (thestochasticparrot.com, Sept 27) concluded the question is contested: no recording settles which account is accurate, and wire outlets (AP, Reuters, The Hill, Guardian, HuffPost) declined to characterize the crowd at all. So the article's headline claim is half-right: booing did occur and is documented, but the evidence does not support presenting it as the stadium's dominant response — cheers were also audible and possibly comparable. No established fact-checker (Snopes, PolitiFact, FactCheck.org, Reuters/AP Fact Check) has rated this claim.

sources.name: USA Today For The Win (booing doubted)

trending_context: A trending partisan dispute: the Daily Beast reported 'a roar of boos audible over scattered applause' while Breitbart reported 'a roar of approval' for the same moment; an independent audit catalogued 23 sources on the contradiction.

headline: Natalie Harp Pulls Trump's Attention to Laptop During Sold-Out Tennessee-Texas Game
trending_claim: During the Sept. 26 Tennessee-Texas game, Trump's executive assistant Natalie Harp held up a laptop that pulled Trump's attention away from the field, with Trump leaning across Sen. Bill Hagerty to look at the screen.
rating_explained: The story asserts Reuters photographs show Harp holding up a laptop for Trump and Hagerty to see, with Trump leaning across Hagerty for a closer look. The named-source evidence confirms this exactly: a Reuters photo by Jonathan Ernst is captioned 'US president Donald Trump looks at a laptop held by his executive assistant Natalie Harp alongside Tennessee senator Bill Hagerty during the Tennessee-Texas game at Neyland Stadium' (republished by People magazine's coverage). An AP photo by Julia Demaree Nikhinson shows the same scene: 'White House aide Natalie Harp, left, holds up a laptop for Trump, right, and Sen. Bill Hagerty, R-Tenn., center, during the game.' The article's 'human printer' background on Harp is attributed to the Washington Post, which reported she frequently supplies Trump with printed news stories and posts to his Truth Social account — corroborated by reporting on her official role as special assistant/executive assistant and the 'human printer' nickname. Crucially, the article does not overreach: it states plainly 'what exactly was on the screen remains unknown,' 'there is no reliable basis for answering that question,' and 'anything beyond that would be guesswork.' The factual claim checks out and the speculation is explicitly withheld, so despite the sensational headline framing, the piece's central claim is accurate. No established fact-checker has rated this claim.

sources.name: AP photo (Julia Demaree Nikhinson, via europesays)

trending_context: Reuters photographs of the moment went viral online, amplified by a Times of India video and Daily Beast coverage of Harp ('human printer'); the article itself notes what was on the screen is unknown and speculation is guesswork.
